content: {"rule": "K-C", "applies": "yes", "applies_why": "The judge resolves the Matthew 1:16 collision by finding the verse's own Greek admits both readings, which is a verse-level ambiguity assessment rather than a chain-against-chain footing analysis.", "verdict": "BREACH", "quote": "D1 vs C2 (Matthew 1:16): UNDERDETERMINED -- the passive egennēthē (was born) with feminine hēs (of whom) admits both the withheld-father and the birth-narration readings; the defender answered the beget-pattern and naming witnesses in [CR3] LINK 4 and [CR2] §5, and the challenger answered hēs in [DR3] C2.", "rule_words": "When the witnesses pressed against a link are the pressing side's own chain read together, the collision weighs chain against chain by footing, never verse by verse; that no one of them states the contrary in its own words is the stating-verse test DG-61 retires, at a judge's seat as at a debater's, for either side.", "room": "The phrase 'weighs chain against chain by footing, never verse by verse' and the retired 'no one of them states the contrary' test: I weighed (1) allowing the judge to call a single verse underdetermined because its Greek admits two readings against (2) requiring the pressed chain and opposing chain to be weighed together by footing.", "why": "The judge's stated basis is the ambiguity of Matthew 1:16's own wording, not a chain-against-chain comparison by footing, so it uses the verse-by-verse approach K-C forbids."}
